samf-senior-2006-r2-01.title: Convert units
samf-senior-2006-r2-01.body:
$7$ km $=7\times10^6$ mm. Dividing by $0.1$ mm per year gives $7\times10^7$ years, which is $70$ million.

**Answer: (C) 70 million**

samf-senior-2006-r2-01.title: Per 10 years
samf-senior-2006-r2-01.body:
Each $10$ years adds $1$ mm. $7$ km is $7000$ m $=7\,000\,000$ mm, so it takes $10\times7\,000\,000=70\,000\,000$ years.

**Answer: (C) 70 million**

samf-senior-2006-r2-02.title: Pick a weight
samf-senior-2006-r2-02.body:
Let $J=80$. Then $75\%$ of $J$ is $60$, and this is $120\%$ of $E$, so $E=50$. The ratio is $\frac{50}{80}=\frac58$.

**Answer: (A) $\frac58$**

samf-senior-2006-r2-03.title: Same height ratio
samf-senior-2006-r2-03.body:
The top two rectangles share the same height, so their widths are in ratio $6:16$. The bottom two rectangles have the same widths as them (and equal heights), so their areas are also in ratio $6:16$, i.e. $x:32=6:16$ gives $x=12$.

**Answer: (E) 12**

samf-senior-2006-r2-03.title: Cross products
samf-senior-2006-r2-03.body:
If the widths are $w_1,w_2$ and the heights $h_1,h_2$, then $w_1h_1=6$, $w_2h_1=16$, $w_2h_2=32$. The unknown is $w_1h_2=\dfrac{w_1h_1\cdot w_2h_2}{w_2h_1}=\dfrac{6\cdot32}{16}=12$.

**Answer: (E) 12**

samf-senior-2006-r2-04.title: Use the diameter
samf-senior-2006-r2-04.body:
Let each ball have diameter $d$. The container has length $3d$ and circumference $\pi d$, so the ratio is $3:\pi\approx3:3.14\approx1:1$.

**Answer: (A) 1:1**

samf-senior-2006-r2-04.title: Plug in numbers
samf-senior-2006-r2-04.body:
Take $d=1$: length $3$, circumference $\pi\approx3.14$. The ratio $3:3.14$ is very close to $1:1$ and not to any other option.

**Answer: (A) 1:1**

samf-senior-2006-r2-05.title: Factorise $75$
samf-senior-2006-r2-05.body:
$75=3\times5\times5$. No digit can be a multiple of $15$ or $25$, so the prime factors $3,5,5$ cannot be merged into fewer digits that are at most $9$: the digits must include $3$, $5$, $5$. The fourth digit must be $1$ (any larger digit would change the product). So the digits are $1,3,5,5$ and their sum is $14$.

**Answer: (C) 14**

samf-senior-2006-r2-05.title: Check by trying other digits
samf-senior-2006-r2-05.body:
Three digits must multiply to $75$ together with the fourth digit being $1$: the only way to write $75$ as a product of three digits is $3\cdot5\cdot5$ (since $5$ cannot be paired with $3$ or $5$ to make a digit). With the extra digit $1$ the sum is $3+5+5+1=14$.

**Answer: (C) 14**

samf-senior-2006-r2-06.title: Check each statement
samf-senior-2006-r2-06.body:
Multiplying $b^2=b+1$ by $b$: $b^3=b^2+b$, so (A) is true. Then $b^3=(b+1)+b=2b+1$, so (C) is true. Multiplying by $b^2$: $b^4=b^3+b^2=b^3+b+1$, so (B) is true. From $b^2-b=1$ we get $b(b-1)=1$, so $b=\frac1{b-1}$, and (E) is true. Finally (D) would say $b^3=b+1-b^2=0$, which is false since $b\ne0$ (as $0\neq0+1$).

**Answer: (D)**

samf-senior-2006-r2-08.title: Rotation between views
samf-senior-2006-r2-08.body:
The faces next to $Q$ are $A$ and $C$ (first view) and $E$ and $A$ (third view). So $A$, $C$, $E$ are all adjacent to $Q$, and $C$ and $E$ are opposite each other (they are on opposite sides of $A$ around $Q$). The two remaining faces are $B$ and $D$; one is opposite $Q$ and the other is adjacent. In the second view, $B$ is on top and $D$ in front, with $C$ on the right. Going from the first view to the second, the cube is turned $180^\circ$ about the axis through $C$ (both $Q$ and $A$ disappear), so $Q$ is now at the bottom and the face on top, $B$, is opposite to $Q$.

**Answer: (B) $B$**

samf-senior-2006-r2-08.title: Orientation check
samf-senior-2006-r2-08.body:
Put $Q$ on top and use coordinates: $Q=+z$, and from view 1, $A=-y$ (front) and $C=+x$ (right). In view 3, $A$ is on the right and $Q$ on top, so the cube has been turned a quarter turn about the vertical axis taking $-y$ to the right; the face now in front is the one that was on the left, so $E=-x$ (opposite $C$). The faces $B$ and $D$ are therefore $+y$ and $-z$ in some order. In every view the three visible faces (top, front, right) appear in the same rotational sense, so the triple (top, front, right) must have the same orientation as $(+z,-y,+x)$. View 2 shows $(B,D,C)$ with $C=+x$. Trying $B=+y$, $D=-z$ gives the triple $(+y,-z,+x)$, which has the opposite orientation, so it is impossible. Hence $B=-z$, $D=+y$, and $B$ is opposite $Q$.

**Answer: (B) $B$**

samf-senior-2006-r2-10.title: Arithmetic progression
samf-senior-2006-r2-10.body:
The angles are $75,75+d,75+2d,75+3d$ and add to $360^\circ$, so $300+6d=360$ and $d=10$. The second largest is $75+20=95^\circ$.

**Answer: (C) 95**

samf-senior-2006-r2-10.title: Use the average
samf-senior-2006-r2-10.body:
The average of the four angles is $90^\circ$, halfway between the two middle angles. If the common difference is $d$, the middle angles are $90\pm\frac d2$ and the smallest is $90-\frac{3d}2=75$, so $d=10$. The second largest angle is $90+\frac d2=95^\circ$.

**Answer: (C) 95**

samf-senior-2006-r2-11.title: Find a suitable square
samf-senior-2006-r2-11.body:
If he was $x$ years old in the year $x^2$, he was born in $x^2-x$. Since he lived entirely in the 1800s, the year $x^2$ lies between $1800$ and $1899$. The only square in that range is $43^2=1849$ ($42^2=1764$ and $44^2=1936$). So he was $43$ in $1849$, and was born in $1849-43=1806$.

**Answer: (A) 1806**

samf-senior-2006-r2-11.title: Test the options
samf-senior-2006-r2-11.body:
The birth year must be of the form $x^2-x=x(x-1)$ with $x^2$ in the 1800s. Checking the options: $1806=42\cdot43$ fits; $1822,1830,1851,1853$ are not products of two consecutive integers (the nearby products are $41\cdot42=1722$, $42\cdot43=1806$ and $43\cdot44=1892$).

**Answer: (A) 1806**

samf-senior-2006-r2-12.title: Maximise the height
samf-senior-2006-r2-12.body:
Take the side of length $20$ as base. The other two sides sum to $52$. The height is greatest when the apex is as high as possible, which happens when the triangle is isosceles with equal sides $26$ (the apex lies on an ellipse with the base endpoints as foci, and is highest at the top of the ellipse). Then the height is $\sqrt{26^2-10^2}=24$ and the area is $\frac12\cdot20\cdot24=240$.

**Answer: (A) 240**

samf-senior-2006-r2-12.title: Heron's formula
samf-senior-2006-r2-12.body:
Let the other sides be $a$ and $b$ with $a+b=52$. The semi-perimeter is $s=36$, so the area is $\sqrt{36\cdot16\cdot(36-a)(36-b)}$. With $(36-a)+(36-b)=20$ fixed, the product $(36-a)(36-b)$ is largest when both equal $10$ (AM-GM), giving area $\sqrt{36\cdot16\cdot100}=6\cdot4\cdot10=240$.

**Answer: (A) 240**

samf-senior-2006-r2-13.title: Any $x$ with fractional part below $\frac12$
samf-senior-2006-r2-13.body:
If $x=n+f$ with $n$ an integer and $0\le f<\frac12$, then $\lfloor x\rfloor=n$ and $x+\frac12=n+f+\frac12<n+1$, so $\lfloor x+\frac12\rfloor=n$ as well. So every such $x$ is a solution, and there are infinitely many.

**Answer: (E) infinite**

samf-senior-2006-r2-13.title: Test numbers
samf-senior-2006-r2-13.body:
$x=0$, $x=0.1$, $x=0.25$, $x=1.3$ all satisfy the equation (both sides $0$, $0$, $0$, $1$). A continuum of solutions exists, so the number is infinite.

**Answer: (E) infinite**

samf-senior-2006-r2-14.title: Divide each term by 9
samf-senior-2006-r2-14.body:
Each term is $9\times$ a repunit: $9=9\cdot1$, $99=9\cdot11$, $999=9\cdot111,\dots$. So the average of the nine numbers is $\frac{9(1+11+111+\cdots+111111111)}{9}=1+11+111+\cdots+111111111$. Adding column by column, the units column gives $9$, the tens column $8$, and so on up to $1$ in the hundred-millions column, so the sum is $123456789$. The digit $0$ is missing.

**Answer: (D) 0**

samf-senior-2006-r2-15.title: Two geometric series
samf-senior-2006-r2-15.body:
The $y$-coordinate gets contributions from the north and south legs: $80-20+5-\frac54+\cdots$, a geometric series with first term $80$ and ratio $-\frac14$. Its sum is $\frac{80}{1+\frac14}=64$. The $x$-coordinate comes from the east and west legs: $40-10+\frac{10}{4}-\cdots$, first term $40$ and ratio $-\frac14$, sum $\frac{40}{5/4}=32$.

**Answer: (A) $(32;64)$**

samf-senior-2006-r2-15.title: Fixed point of a four-leg cycle
samf-senior-2006-r2-15.body:
After the four legs $80,40,20,10$ the net displacement is $(40-10,\,80-20)=(30,60)$, and the whole pattern from then on is a copy of the first, scaled by $\frac1{16}$. If $P$ is the final point, $P=(30,60)+\frac1{16}P$, so $P=\frac{16}{15}(30,60)=(32,64)$.

**Answer: (A) $(32;64)$**

samf-senior-2006-r2-16.title: Split into triangles
samf-senior-2006-r2-16.body:
Join the interior point to the five vertices. This splits the pentagon into five triangles whose bases are the sides (length $s$) and whose heights are the five distances. The total area is $\frac12s\cdot(\text{sum of distances})=\frac12s\cdot16=8s$. So $8s=40$ and $s=5$.

**Answer: (D) 5**

samf-senior-2006-r2-16.title: Check with the regular pentagon
samf-senior-2006-r2-16.body:
The answer does not depend on the shape, so test a regular pentagon with the point at its centre: the five distances equal the apothem $a$, so $5a=16$. The area is $\frac12\cdot(5s)\cdot a=\frac12\cdot5s\cdot\frac{16}5=8s=40$, giving $s=5$ again.

**Answer: (D) 5**

samf-senior-2006-r2-17.title: Subtract collinear triples
samf-senior-2006-r2-17.body:
There are $\binom93=84$ ways to choose three points. Those that lie on a line give no triangle: $3$ rows, $3$ columns and $2$ diagonals, so $8$ triples. Hence $84-8=76$ triangles.

**Answer: (D) 76**

samf-senior-2006-r2-17.title: Count by cases
samf-senior-2006-r2-17.body:
Choose $3$ points from the $9$ and exclude lines: $\frac{9\cdot8\cdot7}{6}=84$ choices; the only collinear triples in a $3\times3$ grid are the $8$ full lines (no line contains three points other than these). So $76$.

**Answer: (D) 76**

samf-senior-2006-r2-18.title: Use the centroid
samf-senior-2006-r2-18.body:
The shaded triangle has vertices $D$, the centre of the rectangle $O$ (intersection of the diagonals) and the intersection $G$ of $DE$ with $AC$. In triangle $BCD$, $CO$ and $DE$ are medians (as $O$ is the midpoint of $BD$ and $E$ the midpoint of $BC$), so $G$ is the centroid, and $OG=\frac13OC$. Triangle $DOC$ has area $\frac14$, and triangle $DOG$ has one third of the base $OC$ so its area is $\frac13\cdot\frac14=\frac1{12}$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac1{12}$**

samf-senior-2006-r2-18.title: Coordinates
samf-senior-2006-r2-18.body:
Let $D=(0,0)$, $C=(2,0)$, $B=(2,1)$, $A=(0,1)$ (area $2$). Line $DE$ ($E=(2,\frac12)$) is $y=\frac x4$; diagonal $AC$ is $y=1-\frac x2$; diagonal $DB$ is $y=\frac x2$. They meet $AC$ at $(\frac43,\frac13)$ and $(1,\frac12)$. The shaded triangle $D,(\frac43,\frac13),(1,\frac12)$ has area $\frac12\left|\frac43\cdot\frac12-1\cdot\frac13\right|=\frac16$. Dividing by the rectangle area $2$ gives $\frac1{12}$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac1{12}$**

samf-senior-2006-r2-19.title: Alternating digit sum
samf-senior-2006-r2-19.body:
A number $abcdef$ is divisible by $11$ if $(a+c+e)-(b+d+f)$ is divisible by $11$. The digit total is $22$, so the difference is even; it can only be $0$ or $\pm22$ (impossible), so we need $a+c+e=b+d+f=11$. The triples from $\{1,2,3,4,5,7\}$ summing to $11$ are $\{1,3,7\}$ and $\{2,4,5\}$ (and these are complementary). Choose which triple goes in the odd positions ($2$ ways) and arrange each triple ($3!\cdot3!=36$ ways): $2\cdot36=72$.

**Answer: (B) 72**

samf-senior-2006-r2-19.title: Check the triples
samf-senior-2006-r2-19.body:
The triples from $\{1,2,3,4,5,7\}$ with sum $11$ are exactly $\{1,3,7\}$ and $\{2,4,5\}$ (other candidates such as $1+4+6$ and $2+3+6$ need a $6$, and $1+5+5$ repeats a digit). They are complementary, so the digits in positions $a,c,e$ form one of them and the other triple goes in $b,d,f$. That is $2$ choices, times $3!$ orders for each triple: $2\cdot6\cdot6=72$.

**Answer: (B) 72**

samf-senior-2006-r2-20.title: Similar triangles
samf-senior-2006-r2-20.body:
The angles in the figure make triangles $AED$ and $BFA$ similar, and triangles $CFB$ and $DEC$ similar. Hence $\dfrac{BF}{AF}=\dfrac{AE}{DE}=\dfrac35$ and $\dfrac{BF}{CF}=\dfrac{CE}{DE}=\dfrac75$. So $AF=\frac53BF$ and $CF=\frac57BF$. Since $AF+CF=AC=3+7=10$: $\frac53BF+\frac57BF=\frac{50}{21}BF=10$, so $BF=4.2$.

**Answer: (C) 4.2**

samf-senior-2006-r2-20.title: Coordinates
samf-senior-2006-r2-20.body:
Put $E=(0,0)$, $A=(-3,0)$, $C=(7,0)$, $D=(0,-5)$. Since $\angle BAD=90^\circ$ and $AD$ has direction $(3,-5)$, $B$ lies on the line through $A$ with direction $(5,3)$: $B=(-3+5t,\,3t)$. Since $\angle BCD=90^\circ$ and $CD$ has direction $(-7,-5)$, $B$ lies on the line through $C$ with direction $(-5,7)$: $B=(7-5s,\,7s)$. Equating gives $3t=7s$ and $-3+5t=7-5s$, so $s=0.6$ and $B=(4,\,4.2)$. Then $F=(4,0)$ and $BF=4.2$.

**Answer: (C) 4.2**
